Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:163: Now, these two aspects mentioned for acquiring holiness, our holy Torah explains to us at the beginning of Parashat Kedoshim, when it wished to explain how we cleave to Him and His holiness rests upon us: it says, "You shall be holy..." (Leviticus 19:2), and it begins to explain the levels of acquiring holiness, saying, "Every man shall revere his mother and his father" (Leviticus 19:3) — and it is known that his father and mother are the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, as is explained in the Zohar several times (Parashat Lech Lecha 77a). It puts the mother first, since the essential aspect of awe is through her, as explained in the Gate of Awe (ch. 14); and it says "his mother and his father," not "the mother and the father shall you revere," to teach that one should revere his mother in her capacity as mother, and his father in his capacity as father — namely, that they gave him birth and did good for him, and it is fitting that he not vex them and transgress their will and be ungrateful, God forbid.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:164: "And keep My Sabbaths" — we have already explained above that Shabbat is a rectification for the days of the week, since on the day of Shabbat one receives flow and illumination, and during the six weekdays one must rectify his deeds so as to be able to receive the neshamah that comes on the day of Shabbat, which is from Atzilut. It follows that the six weekdays are between two Sabbaths, going out from Shabbat and entering Shabbat, and this order applies even to the creation of the world, as my teacher explains in Pardes Rimonim. It may be to this that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, referred (see Shabbat 118b) in saying, "had Israel kept two Sabbaths, no nation would have ruled over them" — hence "and keep My Sabbaths," with the extra word "et" referring to the six days in between, as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:165: "I am the Lord your God" — this is the bond of the supernal holiness within us, resting upon us through the aforementioned rectification, for through awe one draws the Shechinah upon himself, for she is called "awe" (yirah), and within her the whole of Atzilut dwells; and according to how a person prepares himself for awe, so holiness dwells upon him, as is explained in the passage from Parashat Yitro. And so too the acquisition of the supernal neshamah through the rectification of the six days is certainly a rectification for causing the Shechinah to rest within him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:166: Corresponding to the aspect of awe explained, King David, peace be upon him, said to his son Solomon (I Chronicles 28:9): "And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father, and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul, for the Lord searches all hearts, and understands all the imaginations of the thoughts; if you seek Him, He will be found by you, but if you forsake Him, He will cast you off forever." This entire verse reveals to us all the aspects we have explained. First it says, "know the God of your father" — this knowledge is to know whom one serves, that He is the Cause of all, the root and source of all worlds, as explained, and this is [the meaning of] "the God of your father," which indicates [divine] providence. And according to the mystical sense, "the God of your father" — through the last attribute, the supernal Godhood is revealed to the lower beings, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:167: "And serve Him with a whole heart" — the intent follows the pattern of "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5), with both the good inclination and the evil inclination (Berachot 9:5), both of which reside in the heart, in the two chambers of the heart, as we explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 5. And when the evil inclination, which resides on the left side of the heart, is subdued beneath the good inclination, then it is a "whole heart" — for the two hearts have become one heart; but if the good inclination wishes to direct itself toward holiness, and the evil inclination accuses it, they are two separate hearts, and this is not wholeness. It is possible to explain this in the mystical sense too, but we do not wish to depart from our discourse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:168: "And a willing soul" — this will be explained to you by what is explained in the Gate of Love, chapter 4, regarding "for he was delighted with (chafetz) Jacob's daughter" (Genesis 34:19) — there it explains the matter of "the desire of the heart," which is the complete yearning after divine service. "And understands all the imaginations of the thoughts" — our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained this, as we quoted their wording in the Gate of Love, chapter 8.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:169: "If you seek Him, He will be found by you" — here it teaches what we explained from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Parashat Yitro 69a), that whoever wishes to draw down the supernal spirit needs awe and a broken heart, as explained — this is "if you seek Him," for seeking is required until "He will be found by you," in the manner of "and you shall inquire and investigate" (Deuteronomy 13:15), and likewise "Moses diligently sought" (Leviticus 10:16) — since it does not say "if you seek Him, He shall be found for him," but "for you." One might explain "seeking" as the Radak explains in his Sefer HaShorashim, that it is [a term of] preparation, in the manner of "I was sought by those who did not ask" (Isaiah 65:1), the intent being "I was found and I was made available"; and likewise, "sought out by all who desire them" (Psalms 111:2) — prepared and available, and so on. So too, when a person prepares himself and readies himself to receive holiness, the Holy One, blessed be He, will be found for him; but if he does not prepare himself properly, the Holy One, blessed be He, will not be found toward him. And from the fact that it says "He will be found" and not "He will be sought for you," it teaches what they said (Yoma 39a), "whoever comes to be purified, they assist him" — for being found is more significant than seeking. And in saying "for you," the meaning is: on your part, He must be found for you, but He Himself is always available.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:170: "But if you forsake Him, He will cast you off forever" — this is like what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yerushalmi, end of Berachot; Midrash Shmuel): "If [you forsake Me] one day, I will forsake you two days" — a parable of two friends who were beside each other; one turned to his way, a day's journey to the east, and the other likewise turned to his way, a day's journey to the west — behold, between them is a journey of two days; this is [the meaning of] "two days I will forsake you" — this is "He will cast you off forever." Further, "He will cast you off forever" may mean that he will not be among the supernal ones called "servants of the Lord," as explained in the Zohar — for the reason that only those who are always attached in thought ascend there, as explained in chapter 4. Therefore, when a person begins to take hold of holiness and cleave to his Maker for one day, he should follow it with another day, because it will be doubly difficult for him to regain the attachment he had. And as they said, of blessed memory, "if you forget, you shall surely be forgotten" (Deuteronomy 8:19) — if a person forgets a little, they cause him to forget a great deal — this is [the meaning of] "forsake Him," even a small forsaking; and it does not say "if you cast Him off," but "He will cast you off forever," for the reason stated, following the pattern of "if one day you forsake Me..."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:171: Among the further things that cause the holiness of thought, King Solomon, peace be upon him, revealed to us in saying, "Commit your works unto the Lord, and your thoughts shall be established" (Proverbs 16:3), and the intent is several things, all pertaining to the holiness of thought.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:172: The first, according to its plain sense, is in the manner of "cast your burden upon the Lord" (Psalms 55:23), which is explained in the Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 26b) to mean "your burden" is a load — the intent being the load of worldly matters, such as a person's providing for his household and its sustenance and his business dealings, and that he should cast them upon the Lord, in whose hand it is to arrange everything — for all these things confuse a person's thought. Therefore it says, "Commit your works unto the Lord," and by this "your thoughts shall be established" — and this is one of the qualities of trust (bitachon), as is elaborated in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Trust, Introduction), which is rest of the soul from worldly mishaps, and from traveling on the roads and the like — that he trusts in his Master that his sustenance will not be lacking, as it is said, "The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want" (Psalms 23:1), for YHVH, who created him, knows his situation for his good, as King David, peace be upon him, said, "like a weaned child with his mother, my soul is with me" (Psalms 131:2). And when a person strengthens himself in trust in Him, blessed be He, it will be a great cause for the purification of thought, for since he casts all his matters upon the Lord, he has no other thought except that very thing he is occupied with — prayer, or Torah, or a commandment — all of it for divine service without any ulterior motive.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:173: This is the plain meaning of the verse, meaning: "Commit your works unto the Lord" refers to the health of the limbs of his body, in the manner of "He made you and established you" (Deuteronomy 32:6), as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain (Bereshit Rabbah 12:1): the Holy One, blessed be He, and His court, were counted over each and every limb, and so on. And "commit... unto the Lord" means that even though a person's limbs and body are physical, when he commits them and binds them to their root, which is YHVH, the limbs will be refined and the thoughts established. Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains this matter in several ways, that YHVH is found alluded to in the limbs of a person; they say in the Tikkunim (131b), in these words: YHVH is found in every single limb — it is found in the four colors of the hair, and in the four colors of the eye, and in the four folds of the ear, and in the four colors of the face, and in the voice, in speech, in reading and in saying, and in the doing of the hands, and in every single limb of the body — He is YHVH, and so on — so far his words, as pertains to us; and the rest of his wording we quoted in the Gate of Awe.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:174: Further, they explain in the Tikkunim that the Name YHVH is found in a person's body — Yod in the head, Heh-Heh in the arms, Vav in the body. In these words (128b): come and see, He is the head, He is the measure of the eyes, of the ears, of the face, of the two nostrils; measure in the mouth; "the holy shekel" — this is Vav, the shekel of the body; "the wings (kanfei) of the shekel" are the five fingers of the right hand and the five of the left; and because the Name YHVH is measure, size, and weight, the verse says, "You shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in measure, in weight, or in measurement" (Leviticus 19:35) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:175: Further, they explain in the Tikkunim (68b) that the Name spelled out with alephs, Yod-Kei Vav-Kei, is found alluded to in the limbs of a person, in these words: and therefore the right leg, which has three joints, is bound together with the right arm, for a Heh rests within it; and likewise the left arm with the left leg, in which a Heh rests; and likewise body and Covenant are Vav-Vav, and in them rests an Aleph, which is Imma, and it becomes [together, numerically] thirteen and Vav. Yod rests in the ten fingers of the hands and the ten toes of the feet, because the beginning of the holy Name rests from Chochmah, which is in the fingers; the supernal Keter rests in the head of a person, where the hidden thought is — and just as thought is hidden, so it is hidden — so far his words. And it further says: the four elements of the body, in which YHVH rests — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:176: Further, in the Tikkunim in manuscript (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 114b), it says that every single limb in a person is comprised of ten, alluding to the Name Yod-Kei Vav-Kei, and it is said of him, "Let us make man" (Genesis 1:26), for "Adam" is nine by the small reckoning (mispar katan), and the Shechinah is the form of Adam completing the tenth aspect in every single limb. At the end of his words it says: this is the lower Shechinah, which is the completion of those above and below, and so it proceeds through every single limb and every single sefirah; and it says, "Let us make man," until the Shechinah is comprised in all the sefirot and in every limb — at that time all the limbs are completed within her, each one to ten, in this manner: Yod-Kei Vav-Kei; afterward it descends to four, and so on — this requires study there — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:177: Now, after presenting these passages, the verse can be explained in two aspects, both pertaining to practice. The first: "Commit your works unto the Lord" — since one knows that all his limbs, which are called "works" as explained, are sealed with the Name YHVH, he must not sin with them, as the verse says, "You shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in measure, in weight, or in measurement" (Leviticus 19:35), and it explains that these four measures correspond to the Name YHVH: judgment — Yod, measure — Heh, weight — Vav, measurement — Heh. And Rashbi, peace be upon him, says just before the passage we quoted (Tikkunim 128b): and therefore, "you shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in measure," and so on — "measure" here is the measure of the stature (shiur komah), for whoever is not a person of [proper] measures diminishes the supernal stature, and is not sustained from there — for the ten supernal sefirot all proceed by measure from the side of the letter Yod, and by weight from the side of the letter Vav; the two pans of the scale (moznei hashekel) are Heh-Heh — so far his words. And once the limbs are clean and are a throne for YHVH, the thoughts will be established, as explained above in chapter 6 — that the supernal Thought rests only upon a whole and properly rectified throne.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:178: And so, when he considers that the brains in his head contain an allusion to the Name YHVH, and the four brains correspond to the Name YHVH, corresponding to the four portions in the tefillin, which are called the Name YHVH, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Mishpatim 119b), it is fitting that he purify his thoughts — and this is included in "commit your works unto the Lord," meaning that the Name YHVH is alluded to in every single limb of a person, and particularly, in the four brains it is alluded to even more.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:179: Further, this matter is explained at greater length: Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains there (130a) four aspects — sight, hearing, smell, speech — and it further says: there is no rectification of these four letters that does not include the ten sefirot, which are Yod-Kei Vav-Kei; and the four letters that are YHVH do not change in any place — He hears (shomea) to the left, to Israel, and looks (mistakel) to the right upon them, and in the south He hovers (merachef) over them — this is what is written, "and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters" (Genesis 1:2) — and in the west He speaks (memalel) with them; changes are only in the vessels of the body, but in Him there is no change at all — this is what is written, "I am the Lord, I do not change" (Malachi 3:6). And every single limb, which is a lamp for every commandment, a person must set the Holy One, blessed be He, as king over it and prepare a clean and pure place for Him to rest there; and therefore a person must clear away from every single limb all thoughts and all evil, filthy imaginings, which are kelipot, and must call them by all the commandments that rest on every single limb, which are lamps — for every commandment is called a lamp, this being what is written, "for the commandment is a lamp" (Proverbs 6:23), "the lamp of the Lord is the soul of man" (Proverbs 20:27) — so far his words, as pertains to us. What it says, "He hears to the left..." and "in the west He speaks..." is explained above this passage and does not pertain to our subject.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:180: What emerges from the general plain sense of the passage is that a person must rectify all his limbs so that they become a throne upon which the Name YHVH rests, which is the neshamah resting within; and any blemish in any limb causes the Name YHVH to withdraw, as explained further there, and we quoted the entire passage in the Gate of Awe, chapter 9 — see there. This is [the meaning of] "Commit your works unto the Lord," as explained, and by this "your thoughts shall be established" — that is, the Name of thought, Yod-Kei Vav-Kei, which is the inner neshamah spreading through the limbs.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:181: Particularly in light of what was explained above from the passage of Rashbi, peace be upon him, at the end of Tikkun 22 (68b), that the Name of Thought, Yod-Kei Vav-Kei, is alluded to in the limbs of a person, one might read it as "commit unto YHVH" simply — the intent being: commit unto this Name your works, the limbs that are alluded to in this Name, "and your thoughts shall be established" — for when the limbs are purified so that the Name rests within them, the thoughts will be established, since this Name is bound with thought, as has been explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:182: And with this, this chapter is concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:1: We have already explained in chapter 7, in the name of Rashbi, that the brain has four faculties as its chariot — sight, hearing, smell, speech — and he says in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 234a) that these four correspond to the four letters of YHVH; he says: the brain has four living creatures, which are the Throne of Mercy, and what are they? Sight, hearing, smell, speech. Sight — the lion; hearing — the ox; smell — the eagle; and each has four faces and four wings. Speech — man; it grasps above and below — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:2: Now, having explained in the preceding chapters the holiness of the brain and the heart, both of which are bound together regarding fantasy, as we have explained, let us now come to explain, in this chapter, what pertains to the holiness of sight. We begin explaining the matter of sight after explaining the holiness of the heart, for they are connected and dependent on one another — "the heart and the eye are two brokers of transgression" (Yalkut, part 1, remez 750), as we have explained. Regarding the particulars of the eye, we shall quote everything found in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, explaining the particulars of the eye — and when a person knows the place of this allusion in the supernal chariot, he will sanctify his sight properly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:3: Regarding the three colors of the eye, the pupil (bat ayin), and the eyelids, it is explained in Tikkun 4 (18b), in these words: "In the beginning" — it is written, "Open for me the gates of righteousness, I will enter through them, I will give thanks to the Lord" (Psalms 118:19). "Open for me" — certainly, these are the two eyelids that open and close, and concerning them it is said, "and the cherubim shall spread their wings on high" (Exodus 25:20) — these cherubim are the two cherubs of the eye, "spreading their wings" being the eyelids. Further, "open for me the gates of righteousness" — these are the two eyes; when they are on a straight path, it is said of them, "and their faces one toward another" (Exodus 25:20); and when they do not look in a straight path, behold the twisting serpent is there, concerning which it is said, "for death shall part [me and you]" (Ruth 1:17). The three colors of the eye are the three Patriarchs, of whom it is said, "these are the heads of their fathers' houses" (Exodus 6:14). The pupil (bat ayin), which is fine and small, is the Shechinah, joined with the limbs, and concerning her it is said, "keep me as the pupil, the daughter of the eye" (Psalms 17:8), and all is in the mystery of "In the beginning" (Bereshit) — there is "reishit" (beginning/heads), there is "bat" (daughter/pupil) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:4: The two eyelids of the eye that open and close are explained (Ra'aya Meheimna, Parashat Ki Tetzei 280b) to be Netzach and Hod. And what it says regarding "the cherubs of the eye" and "the eyelids of the eye" is further explained in the Tikkunim (128a), in these words: and further, the eye is like the body — its two cherubs are like the two legs, and the two eyelids of the eye correspond to the two arms; these cover, and those fly — so far his words. It appears that the lower folds within the eye are called "cherubim," and the eyelids are the upper ones covering the eye.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:5: Regarding the pupil (bat ayin), it says in the Tikkunim (end of 51a) that the pupil is "the daughter" (bat) from "In the beginning" (bereshit), comprised of the ten "sayings," and she is the black pupil, of whom it is said, "I am black, but comely" (Song of Songs 1:5), and through her light shines — this is what is written, "and Torah is light" (Proverbs 6:23) — so far his words, in brief.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:6: And in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Ki Tetzei 280b) it is explained how the Name YHVH is found in the eye, in these words: the Holy Lamp [Rashbi] said to him: Yod is the pupil of the eye, [as it says] "for the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light"; Heh, Vav — that shine within it; Heh — the three colors, the appearance of the eye, and the two wings of the eye; five lights shine within it internally, the supernal Heh, which is light — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:7: Further, in the Tikkunim (end of 128a), in these words: the eyes in roundness are from the side of the letter Yod, in length from the side of the letter Vav; the wings of the eye are Heh-Heh; in these four letters the eye is in measure and in weight — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:8: Further, regarding the details of the eye, they explain in the Tikkunim (128a), in these words: further, "and their rims (gabhen)" — these are the seven layers of the eye, one over the other like the layers of onions; "and height (govah) to them" — this is the eye, which comprises all colors; "and their rims were full of eyes" (Ezekiel 1:18) — these are the wings of the eye and the eyelids of the eye, for there are four colors in the eye corresponding to the four faces of each living creature, and the two wings of the eye, which are the eyelids, and the two cherubs of the eye correspond to the four wings of each living creature; and in these four colors of the eye shine the four letters YHVH, and in the four wings of the eye shines Adonai — this is [the meaning of] "for one high one watches over another that is high" (Ecclesiastes 5:7), "and there are higher ones over them" — these are YHVH, Ehyeh, Abba, Imma — so far his words. The intent, in brief, is that in the eyelids and wings of the eye, two in each eye, correspond to the four wings of the living creatures, which are the Name Adonai; and the four colors correspond to the Name YHVH; and the light shining in the eyelids is YHVH and Ehyeh, Abba and Imma.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:9: Further, there, further on: the cherubs of the eye and the eyelids of the eye — concerning them it is said, "and the cherubim shall spread their wings on high, covering the covering (kaporet) with their wings" (Exodus 25:20) — this is the covering (kapparah) of the eye. The three colors of the eye are Ehyeh, YHVH, Adonai — general, particular, and general — indicated by the acrostic "Yichud, Berachah, Kedushah" (Unity, Blessing, Holiness), and the sign "Ya'aneinu Beyom Kor'einu" ("May He answer us on the day we call"), for these three Names total, numerically, Yavak (112). Ehyeh — the supernal Keter; YHVH — the middle pillar; Adonai — the lower Shechinah. Adonai is general; Ehyeh is particular; YHVH is [both] particular and general — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:10: Further, they explain in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 96b) that in the eye is YHVH and Yod-Kei Vav-Kei, in these words: and some explain them thus, in the ten letters of the explicit Name — in the seven layers of the eye and the three colors of the eye shine ten letters, which are Yod-Kei Vav-Kei, and this is "and the likeness of the face of a man"; in the two cherubs of the eye and the two eyelids of the eye shine the four faces of man, which are YHVH, of whom it is said, "and the likeness of their faces was the face of a man" (Ezekiel 1:10) — the likeness of the three living creatures is the likeness of the faces of man — so far their words. Though this is said there regarding the details of the eye of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, nevertheless it is possible to learn from it also for ourselves, since Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains in the Tikkunim (130a), whose wording we quoted above (ch. 7), that sight, hearing, smell, and speech each contain YHVH and Yod-Kei Vav-Kei, though it was not explained there how — and it is possible to understand it from what is explained in this passage.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:11: When you examine carefully the Names that Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains regarding the eye, you will find in the eye the entirety of the whole "stature" (shiur komah), particularly in the three Names Yavak; and you already know what the commentators explained, that the pupil of the eye is called "ishon" ("little man") because the form of a small man is seen within it, and it seems by this reason that the appearance of the form of a man within it is for the reason stated — that the form of the whole stature, in the aforementioned Names, is portrayed and concealed there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:12: And so they further explain there in the Tikkunim (128a), regarding the details of the eye, that it contains an allusion to the whole body, as we quoted its wording above, saying, "the two cherubs are like the two legs, the two eyelids of the eye correspond to the two arms"; and it further says there, corresponding to the wings of the eye are the two lips that open and close, and corresponding to them the two wings of the lung, and the eye corresponds to the heart, which is a burning fire, and so on — behold, an allusion to the whole of a person in the eye.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:13: Further, there is in it an allusion to the whole world, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi 226a), that the white surrounding the whole eye is an allusion to the Ocean Sea that surrounds the whole world; the second color is the dry land and the water within it; the third is Jerusalem, standing in the middle of the world; the fourth color, which is the pupil, from which the light emerges, is the point of Zion, the Foundation Stone in the Temple of the Holy of Holies, from which the world was founded, and there the Shechinah rested and from there her light went out to the world; and this same matter is explained in the Tikkunim (126b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:14: Let us return to the matter: since the eye contains an allusion to all the aforementioned holy Names, and the whole "stature," and the whole world, whoever guards his eyes from sinning with them guards his whole body and sustains the world by his merit; and if, God forbid, he causes a blemish with them, he causes a blemish in all that has been mentioned. Therefore it is fitting that a person not look at a place of nakedness with his eyes. The essence of the blemish is in the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, for he blemishes the holy sight that emerges from Tiferet, coming forth from the pupil, which is the Shechinah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:15: Even regarding permissible matters, one must not satiate his eye — for so Ra'aya Meheimna explains, that any sight that is not of Torah or a commandment, the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah do not rest there, in these words, in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas, end of 229b): sight and hearing where there is no Torah and mitzvah — the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah do not rest there; for the Holy One, blessed be He, rests in sight, and so His Shechinah, in Torah — "and Torah is light" — the sight of His Shechinah, YHVH — "in a vision I make Myself known to him" (Numbers 12:6), His Shechinah is known — so far his words. The intent is that in sight alone one finds an allusion to the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah — an allusion to the Holy One, blessed be He, is that she is called "Torah is light"; an allusion to His Shechinah is that the verse says "in a vision I make Myself known to him," and "vision" (mar'ah) is the Shechinah, as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Ki Tetzei 280b). It is possible to say that this is the aspect of the pupil, which is the "vision" through which the supernal light comes forth glorified.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:16: Among the rectifications of the eyes is what the verse says, "and the humble of eye He shall save" (Job 22:29), which brings about shame and humility. So too the will of Ramban to his son: "Do not look upon another's face when speaking to him." And so it is explained in the Midrash, in these words: Rabbi Acha bar Yoshiah says, do not look upon women, so that you not come to speak of nakedness; and the Sages say, whoever has shame of face does not quickly sin, as it is said, "and that His fear may be before your faces, that you sin not" (Exodus 20:17); and whoever has no shame of face quickly sins, as it is said, "the show of their countenance testifies against them" (Isaiah 3:9) — so far their words. It must be that shame of face comes about because one is humble of eye; for if one is haughty of eye, he certainly has no shame of face. By this we understand the connection between the Sages' words and Rabbi Acha bar Yoshiah's words: the Sages came to add to his words, saying that not only will one not come to speak of nakedness, but this will also cause him shame of face; and whoever has this does not quickly sin, even a minor sin; and whoever does not have shame of face — since haughtiness of the eyes indicates brazenness of face — quickly sins.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:17: Know that for the rectification of thought, one must be humble of eye, and by this he rectifies his thought in every aspect — whether by not looking at women (a woman he has not seen, he will not come to think of her), and even regarding permissible things, such as colored garments spread on a wall, as we shall further quote their words, of blessed memory (Avodah Zarah 20b) — for anything a person looks at becomes portrayed, and that image is portrayed in his intellect, and it follows that when he comes to pray or occupy himself with Torah, those physical forms he saw become portrayed in his intellect, causing a blemish and confusion in his thought so that he cannot properly direct his intention — for the eyes see only through the power of the neshamah, and it follows that the power of the neshamah goes outward and absorbs that thing and is imprinted in the brain of imagination, as we explained in chapter 6, that there are three brains; and if the thing he looked at was a matter of nakedness, he has brought nakedness into a high place.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:18: This was the greatness of our father Abraham, peace be upon him, of whom our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bava Batra 16a), on the verse, "Now I know that you are a fair woman to look upon" (Genesis 12:11), that he never looked at his own wife — the reason being, as explained, so as not to draw the power of the neshamah outward and bring a physical thing into his intellect, for it would cause confusion of thought, as explained, mixing the mundane with the holy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:19: Therefore it is fitting for a person, when he wishes to pray, not to look at anyone's face, even a child's, so as not to come to think about matters concerning that person; rather, at the time he prays, he should sanctify himself and think that he has no relation or closeness with any person, only with the Creator of his soul alone — and this will be a great aid to his intention.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:20: But looking at the face of one's teacher is a mitzvah and a rectification for the eyes, for through that gaze one acquires in his soul the illumination of the pure neshamah appearing on his face — particularly the receiving of his face on Shabbat and festivals; and receiving the face of every sage is a rectification for the eyes.
